NBA · NCAA football · 1970–2023

Durable
Dominance

Fourteen franchises won the last forty-three NBA championships. Run the same seasons through a random walk driven by each team's own measured strength and you get twenty. Championships are roughly twice as concentrated as the teams' quality can explain — and the gap is a multi-season effect, not playoff luck.

The clustering is the phenomenon. Champions arrive already decorated — the average winner holds 2.1 prior titles and 5.1 prior top-four finishes, with a 0.571 career record. Only 14 of 43 were first-time winners.

Study A

Do tight leagues crown veterans?

Six measures of how decorated each champion was, against eight measures of how balanced its league was that year. Eighty-four correlations, so they are judged against a false-discovery correction rather than raw p-values.

Both sides drift over time — pedigree counts accumulate mechanically, and expansion changes the spread of records — so each pair is detrended on year before testing. Of 84 pairs, 8 are significant raw and 7 after detrending, against roughly four expected by chance. Three survive Benjamini-Hochberg.

Surviving pedigree × balance correlations pedigree_vs_balance.csv
LeagueChampion pedigree Balance measurer detrendedq
NCAAFprior titlesGini of wins+0.5120.006
NCAAFprior titlesSD of win%+0.4510.017
NCAAFtitles, last 10 yearsGini of wins+0.4570.017

Every surviving measure is oriented so a higher value means a less balanced season. The positive sign therefore reads: less competitive seasons crown more decorated champions. Imbalance and entrenchment travel together — the opposite of the idea that competitive balance reinforces an elite. Nothing survives in the NBA, whose champions are decorated regardless of how tight the league was.

Study B

Championships against a random walk

A postseason is a short random walk. Each series is seven weighted coin flips; win four and advance. Feed in each season's real strengths and you get the title distribution a league should produce if nothing carried across seasons except visible quality.

Strength comes from a Bradley-Terry fit to the complete head-to-head matrix, so a team is credited for who it beat rather than only how often it won. The matrix reconciles exactly with the standings — 82 games per team, zero mismatches.

P(i beats j) = σ( βi − βj + home court )　·　series = best of 7

First, is the model any good?

Scaling every strength gap by a temperature γ and maximising the likelihood of the 43 champions that actually happened gives γ = 1.0 — the raw fitted gaps need no adjustment. The likelihood is flat from 0.8 to 1.4, so this pins the scale only loosely; what matters is that 1.0 sits comfortably inside that range rather than at an edge. The reliability curve is the sharper check, and it holds across the whole range, favourites included.

Reliability 678 playoff team-seasons

Circle area is the number of team-seasons in each probability bin. Points sitting on the dashed line mean the model's stated confidence matches what happened.

Study C

Where does the excess come from?

A puzzle: the simulation already uses real strengths, and its per-season predictions are calibrated. So how can the 43-season record be so much more concentrated?

The resolution

Calibration is a marginal property — each season's probability is right on average. Concentration is a joint one. Both hold at once if championship outcomes are positively correlated across seasons for the same franchise, beyond what measured strength explains. That correlation is exactly what durable dominance means, and it is what the single-season model cannot contain.

Quality is persistent — and already priced in

Lag-1 autocorrelation of team strength is ρ = 0.58, a half-life of about 1.3 seasons. But within-franchise variation (SD 0.61) dwarfs between-franchise variation (SD 0.23): franchises cycle rather than being permanently good. And because the simulation uses each season's real strengths, all of this is already inside it.

Is beating your strength a stable trait?

Splitting the record in half and correlating each franchise's excess titles across the two halves gives r = +0.24, p = 0.23 across 28 franchises. Positive, but not significant — suggestive of a persistent conversion skill, and well short of establishing one.

Is it one era? concentration_by_era.csv

The effect is strongest in 1995–2009 and absent in 2010–2023, where real and simulated counts are identical. Durable dominance in the NBA looks like a 20th-century phenomenon the modern league no longer shows. Individual eras are underpowered at 13–15 seasons, so the full-period test remains the primary one.

Giving every franchise a fixed, persistent strength bonus and sweeping its size, the observed concentration is reproduced at a bonus SD of about 0.38 log-odds — roughly 57% of the within-season spread of team strength itself (0.67). That is a large latent effect, which is itself a reason to treat the single-hidden-trait story sceptically.

Study D

Can machine learning beat the physics?

The simulation is a strong baseline: a generative model with no learned parameters. Trained on 1980–2008 and tested on 2009–2023, can learned models do better at naming the champion?

Predicting the champion, held-out seasons 678 playoff team-seasons · 43 champions

No. The random-walk simulation (0.1713) ties the best learned model (0.1717) and beats the rest. Handing the simulation's own probability to a logistic regression as an extra feature makes it worse — the simulation already contains what the other features carry.

Conference seed leads, then prior top-four finishes and current-season quality. Prior titles contribute nothing and career win% is negative: once you know how good a team is now, its history adds no predictive value.

The tension worth noticing

Study B says the aggregate record is more concentrated than strength explains. Study D says you cannot predict which franchises will beat their strength — a history-only model reaches AUC 0.54 out of sample, and the correlation between prior titles and the simulation residual is +0.06 (p = 0.37). Both results are real. Durable dominance shows up reliably in the aggregate and dissolves when you ask it to name names.

Study F

Do tight regular seasons crown new champions?

Study A asked this as a correlation. Here it is asked the way you would actually phrase it: in the most competitive third of seasons, how often is the champion a historical powerhouse, and how often is it somebody new?

Start with the base rate, which is striking on its own. 71% of NBA champions across 38 seasons had already won a title before, and 67% of college football's across 49. Repeat winners are the norm, not the exception.

Defining both halves

A champion counts as a powerhouse under four escalating definitions: it had won before; it was among the three most decorated teams in the league that season; its career winning percentage sat in the top quartile of its contemporaries; or it already held three or more titles. The middle two are measured relative to the teams it played against — raw title counts grow mechanically as history accumulates, so a fixed threshold would call later champions powerhouses for no reason but the calendar.

Tightness is measured seven ways, including the one the question names — the average team's absolute distance from the median win% — plus the spread of records, of scoring margin, the Gini of wins, the best-to-worst gap, and the rate at which the weaker side actually won its games.

Why not just run all 28 combinations

The seven balance measures are near-duplicates — they correlate at 0.8 to 0.99 with each other, and a single principal component absorbs 82% of their variance in the NBA and 58% in college football. Running 7 × 4 tests and then correcting for 52 comparisons would be both underpowered and misleading. The primary analysis collapses them into one tightness index and runs eight tests, one per league and powerhouse definition, controlling for year. The full grid is kept below as a robustness display.

An odds ratio below 1 means tighter seasons crown fewer established champions. All 8 of 8 point that way, and 2 survive the false-discovery correction — both of them in college football, and both under the strictest definitions of a powerhouse.

The answer, in plain numbers

Take the measure the question names — the average team's distance from the median win% — and split college football's seasons into thirds. In the tightest third, 6% of champions were among the three most decorated programmes in the country. In the loosest third, 59% were. Each standard deviation of extra tightness multiplies the odds of a blue-blood champion by 0.27 (95% CI 0.11–0.66).

Across the whole 7 × 4 robustness grid, 34 of 52 cells show a lower powerhouse rate in tighter seasons. Because the measures are near-duplicates, read that as one consistent pattern rather than 52 independent confirmations.

What this adds

The effect is real but narrow. It shows up in college football, under the strictest definitions of an established champion, and it points the same way in the NBA without reaching significance (odds ratio 0.48 for a three-time champion, p = 0.07 across 38 seasons). That pattern makes sense: college football has no draft, no cap and the widest talent gaps, so a loose season is exactly when the blue bloods should separate. And note what it does not contradict — Study B's excess concentration is a multi-season effect, while this is a within-season one. A league can crown fresh champions in its tightest years and still, across four decades, concentrate titles far more than quality alone explains.

The NFL is absent from this study. This repository has its complete standings from 1970 but no record of who won the title, and a champion cannot be inferred from a regular-season table.

Conclusions

What the record supports

  1. Durable dominance is real and measurable. NBA championships are 1.64× more concentrated than the teams' own measured quality can explain, and every sport tested is 1.7–3.1× more concentrated than chance among its own field.
  2. It is a multi-season effect, not playoff luck. The single-season model is well calibrated; what it misses is the correlation of outcomes across seasons for the same franchise.
  3. The mechanism is not identified. Over-performance does not replicate across halves of history (p = 0.23) and is not predictable out of sample. Continuity of personnel, elite teams coasting in the regular season, playoff-specific quality, and a short 43-season record in which a few unusual runs dominate the statistics all remain live.
  4. Imbalance and entrenchment travel together. Asked as a rate rather than a correlation, all eight primary tests point the same way: tighter regular seasons crown less-established champions. Two survive correction, both in college football under the strictest definitions — in its tightest third of seasons only 6% of champions were among the three most decorated programmes, against 59% in its loosest third. This is the opposite of the idea that competitive balance reinforces an elite.
  5. Within-season and across-season dominance are different things. A league can crown fresh champions in its tightest years (Study F) and still concentrate titles across four decades far more than quality alone explains (Study B). Nothing here requires those to agree.
  6. The modern NBA no longer shows it. 2010–2023 matches its simulation exactly.
What would settle it

Playoff series data. Everything here infers postseason behaviour from regular-season strength; actual series results would let the model be tested where it matters rather than calibrated to one outcome per year. Roster continuity. The leading candidate mechanism — dynasties keeping personnel the standings cannot see — is directly measurable and absent from this data. More leagues with verified champions. The concentration test needs long records to have power, which is why the era splits individually do not reach significance.

Method

Bradley-Terry strengths by penalised MLE on the full head-to-head matrix; 16-team bracket held constant across eras; best-of-7 as the majority of seven weighted Bernoulli draws, which is exact.

Verification

22 tests in tests/, including the simulator checked against the closed-form best-of-7 probability at five parameter settings, and a check that no pedigree measure can see its own season.

Companion

The cross-sport comparison — cycling, golf, tennis, cricket, college football and the Women's World Cup — is in the Cross-Sport Dominance Atlas.
